india-deep-tech-f0a3e458df.headline: Sarvam Gets Backing From Activate As $300 Mn Funding Round Gains Momentum
india-deep-tech-f0a3e458df.fulltext:
- AI-focused venture fund Activate has invested in Sarvam as part of the startup's ongoing $300 million funding round
- The two firms plan to collaborate on AI startups, enterprise adoption and research talent
- Fresh capital will support foundational AI models, computing infrastructure and enterprise deployments
AI-focused venture fund Activate has announced a strategic investment in Bengaluru-based artificial intelligence (AI) startup Sarvam, joining the company's ongoing $300 million fundraising round.
The development comes a day after Sarvam disclosed that it had secured an additional $75 million from investors including Nvidia, Glade Brook Capital and Gaja Capital.
The latest tranche forms part of the startup's planned $300 million raise, which values the company at around $1.5 billion, as per a report by The Economic Times (ET).
Activate has invested about $15 million in Sarvam. The investment represents the fund's third growth-stage bet, following its investments in voice AI startup ElevenLabs and voice dictation company Wispr Flow, the report said.
Sarvam had previously announced the first close of the funding round led by HCLTech, with participation from Bessemer Venture Partners and existing investors Peak XV Partners and Khosla Ventures.
The company plans to use the fresh capital to develop next-generation foundational AI models, expand AI computing infrastructure and accelerate enterprise deployments.
Advertisement
Investment Through Dedicated Growth Vehicle
Activate co-founder and Haptik co-founder Aakrit Vaish said the Sarvam investment was executed through a separate special purpose vehicle rather than the firm's core early-stage fund.
"While its core fund invests in young companies, the Sarvam investment was made through a separate special purpose vehicle (SPV) created for growth-stage opportunities," Vaish said, as per ET.
Highlighting Sarvam's position in India's AI landscape, he said enterprise demand for the company's technology is expected to come from multiple sectors.
"Sarvam is probably the most important company of our generation when we think about AI in India," he added.
Advertisement
Focus On Enterprise AI And Research
Beyond the investment, Activate and Sarvam intend to collaborate in three key areas. These include supporting India's AI startup ecosystem, helping digital-first enterprises deploy AI, and strengthening research talent.
The announcement follows Sarvam's Epoch conference earlier this week, where the startup introduced eight AI offerings spanning coding tools, enterprise AI agents, voice AI, document intelligence and cybersecurity products.
Vaish said these should not be viewed as separate products but as components of a unified enterprise AI platform. He added that most customers are expected to begin with a single capability before gradually expanding their use of the broader platform.

ai-ee6239399c.headline: Anthropic signs $10B deal with AI cloud startup Volta
ai-ee6239399c.fulltext:
Anthropic has been on a cloud partnership spree in recent months, and its latest move is reportedly a $10 billion deal with AI cloud startup Volta.
Bloomberg originally reported that Volta, founded earlier this year, will provide cloud compute to the Claude maker over a six-year period.
Volta has a partner in this deal, Bitdeer, a crypto-mining company that will help develop the data center to provide the compute capacity. That facility will be located in Norway and will deliver a 133 megawatt capacity. It will be fueled by Nvidia’s Vera Rubin systems, the chipmaker’s state-of-the-art AI chip architecture.
Volta is part of Nvidia’s Cloud Partner program, which is a consortium of AI cloud providers that use Nvidia’s GPUs in their data centers.
Volta had spoken about a deal with an AI lab but hadn’t named the specific company it was working with. Bloomberg originally cited anonymous sources familiar with the deal. TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic for more information.
Anthropic has sought to aggressively expand its compute capacity over the last several months as it wages a corporate battle with its competitors. The company also recently announced new compute deals with the likes of SpaceX and Amazon.

world-3bc0540d47.headline: India’s ruling BJP loses byelection in stronghold after Cockroach student protests
world-3bc0540d47.fulltext:
India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party has lost a byelection in a seat it had held for three decades, after the Cockroach movement student protests that have shaken Narendra Modi’s government.
Prashant Kishor, a high-profile electoral strategist turned politician, scored a breakthrough win for his fledgling Jan Suraaj (Good Governance) party in the Bankipur constituency in Patna, the capital of the eastern state of Bihar.
The byelection, in what had been considered a BJP stronghold, was closely watched because it came in the aftermath of nationwide student protests over exam paper leaks that forced the resignation of the education minister, a rare retreat by a government that prides itself on not yielding to public pressure.
Kishor said his victory was a wake-up call for Modi to improve education and create jobs.
The BJP lost two of three byelection contests this week, with the opposition Congress retaining the Datia constituency in central Madhya Pradesh. The BJP comfortably held Manjalpur in Gujarat, Modi’s home state.
Kishor’s supporters said his campaign had succeeded by focusing on issues that resonated with younger voters, particularly education, exams scandals and unemployment.
Deepak Sharma, a former BJP supporter, told the Hindu newspaper: “Unlike other political leaders who make lofty promises, he raised the simple slogan: vote for the future of your children.”
The opposition have said the student protest movement is beginning to dent BJP support among younger voters. Nearly two-thirds of India’s population is under 35. While the official youth unemployment rate is 16%, nearly 40% of graduates aged 15-25 and 20% of those aged 25-29 are jobless, far higher proportions than among the less educated, according to the latest State of Working India report by Azim Premji University.
The BJP’s president, Nitin Nabin, who previously represented Bankipur, described the largely gen Z protesters as “a virus and a cockroach gang devoted to breaking the country” during the byelection campaign.
After he lost the election, he said the party would “undertake a thorough introspection”. Senior BJP sources quoted in the Indian media said the loss has shown that even core supporters could change their minds.
A significant victory for the BJP in West Bengal last year expanded the party’s reach into one of the last major regions outside its control, but that triumph has been followed by a string of political headaches, including the student protests.
The Cockroach Janata party began as an online joke after a senior judge described unemployed young Indians as cockroaches and parasites. It has since morphed into a nationwide movement with 26.6 million Instagram followers, more than the BJP and Congress combined.
The government has also become embroiled in a separate confrontation with the social media company Meta after a video featuring Modi in which he promised to crack down on exam fraud briefly disappeared from Facebook.
The parliamentary committee on communications and information technology has demanded Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, apologise personally and explain how the video vanished. According to local media, Meta executives have already apologised and blamed automated systems designed to detect fake content.
The row has highlighted broader government unease about the influence of foreign technology companies over political discourse. Nishikant Dubey, the chair of the committee, said large parties such as the BJP and Congress often received less visibility online than movements with no formal political status.
“The country needs to understand what Meta, X and YouTube are doing through their algorithms,” Dubey said.
Ajoy Bose, a Delhi-based political analyst, said the Bankipur defeat carried symbolic weight far beyond a single constituency. “Coming as it does after the student protests, the optics look very bad for the BJP. I would not directly connect the result to the protests, but Bihar was one of the main centres of the student agitation, so the two will inevitably be linked in public perception.”
But he cautioned against reading the outcome as evidence of a nationwide shift in voter sentiment. “What’s changing is the perceived invincibility of the BJP’s election machine,” Bose said. “There was a widespread belief the party had every election sewn up.”

india-82363433b5.headline: India moves to give its instant payments network a business model
india-82363433b5.fulltext:
India is taking steps to reshape the business model behind its Unified Payments Interface (UPI), a widely used payments network built by the government, via new legislation that could pave the way for merchants to pay charges on some UPI transactions.
The legislation (PDF) lays the legal groundwork for a potential overhaul of India’s zero-merchant-discount-rate (MDR) regime, under which businesses have not paid fees to accept UPI payments since 2020.
The policy shift comes as UPI has become ubiquitous in India, processing a record 23.66 billion transactions worth ₹29.88 trillion (around $313.4 billion) in July alone, per the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), the operator of UPI.
India scrapped merchant discount rates on UPI transactions in January 2020 to accelerate adoption of the payments network, which instead relied on state incentives to support its operation and development.
The proposal comes after years of argument between the finance ministry, India’s central bank, and payment companies over how to fund the fast-growing network. Banks and fintech firms have argued that the policy of keeping merchant payments free has become harder to sustain as transaction volumes and infrastructure costs climbed.
“For us to get to 90% penetration, and to take UPI global, startups, fintechs and banks will need to fund this expansion through continued investments in IT, innovation and cyber security,” Amrish Rau, chief executive of fintech firm Pine Labs, wrote on X, welcoming the move.
Rau said allowing the industry to recover part of those investments from merchants while keeping consumer and peer-to-peer payments free would put UPI on a more sustainable footing.
The legislation does not itself impose merchant fees or specify which transactions would be affected, leaving those details to be specified later.
Nonetheless, market analysts believe the legislation could mark the first step toward a significant new revenue stream for India’s payments industry. In a report published on Tuesday, Jefferies estimated that introducing merchant charges on higher-value UPI transactions could generate an additional ₹50 billion to ₹100 billion (about $525 million to $1.05 billion) in annual revenue by fiscal 2028, assuming a fee of 15-30 basis points.
Indian daily Economic Times reported last month that officials were considering limiting any merchant charges to larger merchants rather than applying them across all UPI transactions.
In a report last week, brokerage firm Bernstein wrote that such an approach would preserve UPI’s consumer-friendly model while creating a meaningful new revenue pool for banks and payment companies. The report noted that transactions above ₹2,000 (about $21) account for only about 4% of payment volumes but nearly 70% of transaction value.
The legislation will be closely watched by countries where UPI is now live, which include Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, and France.
The law could be particularly significant for companies that dominate India’s digital payments market. Walmart-owned PhonePe and Alphabet’s Google Pay together account for nearly 80% of UPI transaction volumes, according to NPCI data. However, how much either company ultimately benefits will depend on how any merchant fees are distributed among banks, payment apps, and other participants in the ecosystem.

climate-energy-a469a7e341.headline: Brookfield Launches $600 Million India-focused Renewable Energy Platform
climate-energy-a469a7e341.fulltext:
Brookfield Launches $600 Million India-focused Renewable Energy Platform
Brookfield Asset Management announced the launch of Lumara Energy, a new India-based platform focused on accelerating the development and construction of renewable energy projects.
The launch of the new platform comes as India continues to scale up its investments in clean energy, with the country aiming to reach 500 GW of installed renewable energy capacity by 2030. Earlier this year India approved new targets to reduce economy-wide emissions intensity by 47% and to achieve 60% of electric power capacity from non-fossil-based sources by 2035.
According to Brookfield the new platform will deploy approximately $600 million, and will be anchored by an initial development portfolio of over 6 GW of capacity spread across solar, wind and battery storage.
The platform will be anchored by Brookfield’s Catalytic Transition fund (CTF), which was launched in 2023 with a $1 billion anchor commitment from UAE-backed climate investment platform ALTÉRRA, and is aimed at deploying capital into clean energy and transition assets in emerging markets in South and Central America, South and Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe.
In a post announcing the launch of the new platform, Nawal Saini, Managing Partner at Brookfield Asset Management, said:
“India is at an important moment in its energy transition. The renewable energy opportunity here is significant, supported by strong demand growth from commercial and industrial customers, global corporates, hyperscalers and the government.”
Saini said that Lumara will help address key bottlenecks in India’s renewable energy market by support faster project execution and by providing credit solutions to developers, adding that “these are critical as India continues to build renewable capacity at scale.”

world-0d03df74e8.headline: Projectile sinks Indian-flagged ship off Yemen coast
world-0d03df74e8.fulltext:
Projectile sinks Indian-flagged ship off Yemen coast
- Published
An Indian-flagged vessel capsized and sunk after it was hit by a projectile off the coast of Yemen, officials say.
All 14 people on board the MSV Faize Noore Oliya - 13 of which were Indian nationals - were safely rescued, India's Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said.
Sonowal condemned the "unprovoked attack" and said steps would be taken to ensure the safety of seafarers in the region. It is not clear who struck the ship.
It is the latest in a spate of attacks on vessels in the Red Sea, an alternative waterway that some tankers had been using since Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz in February.
India's ministry of external affairs later released a statement calling attacks on commercial shipping in the region "deeply worrisome".
"The targeting of commercial shipping in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways in the region, in keeping with international law, must be restored at the earliest," the ministry said.
Much of the region's shipping routes have been disrupted since the US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
Since then, Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's busiest oil shipping channels, hugely impacting global oil prices.
Some ships carrying oil from Saudi Arabia had instead passed through an alternative shipping lane in the Red Sea, but a recent spate of attacks by Yemen's Houthi fighters on Saudi tankers has further heightened risks in the region.
Yemen's transportation ministry, part of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, accused the Iran-backed Houthis of carrying out the attack by using a boat laden with explosives, Reuters news agency reported.
The group have not commented on the incident.
The Houthis announced what it called a blockade on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports on 20 July.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency has reported several attacks on ships in the region over the past week.
Despite this, oil prices fell to a three-week low on Tuesday as senior US officials raised hopes of a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
In June, the US and Iran agreed on a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to halt military operations and reopen the Strait, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days.
But three weeks after it was signed, US President Donald Trump declared the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on ships in the strait, and US strikes in response.
US officials said on Tuesday that talks have been progressing, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggesting a deal to reopen the Strait could be agreed as soon as Tuesday or Wednesday.
Iran has said it is not negotiating with the US - and has no plans to do so - and is instead talking to Oman.

health-tech-23463c75cc.headline: India Pharma Exports: 2030 Target Cut to $90 Billion
health-tech-23463c75cc.fulltext:
India Pharma Exports Hit a Record. So Why Was the 2030 Target Cut?
Pharmexcil now sees $80-90 billion by 2030, not $130 billion. Tariffs and shipping, not demand, explain the gap.
India pharma exports hit a record $31.1 billion in FY26. Yet Pharmexcil has cut the industry's 2030 target from $130 billion to $80-90 billion. The reason is not weak demand. US tariff uncertainty and Middle East shipping trouble have made exports costlier and harder to plan. Shipments to the US fell nearly 10% to about $9.5 billion.
India pharma exports crossed $31 billion in FY26. That is a record. Yet the industry's own export body just cut its 2030 goal by about a third. Both things are true at once. The gap between them says a lot about where this sector is headed.
What Pharmexcil Actually Said
Namit Joshi chairs the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India (Pharmexcil). In April 2025, the industry set a goal of $130 billion in sales by 2030. Joshi now expects $80 billion to $90 billion instead.
His reason was blunt. "Given the geopolitical changes, the Middle East crisis and everything, I don't foresee us achieving that growth target," he said.
Note what is missing from that list. Demand. Nobody expects the world to need fewer medicines. The problem is what it now costs to ship them and how hard that is to plan.
A Record Year That Still Missed the Mark
India's pharma market was worth about $60 billion in the year to March 2026. Exports made up $31 billion of that. Domestic sales made up $29 billion.
The US market shrank while the total still grew. Brazil, Europe and Africa took up the slack. Growth of just over 2% is thin. But it is growth, with the largest buyer in decline.
Why the US Decides India's Pharma Numbers
One number gets misread all the time. Generics make up about 90% of all prescriptions filled in the US. But those are all generics from every country. Not India's alone.
India's own share is still huge. Indian firms fill close to half of every generic script in the US.
Here is the catch. Generics are cheap. India's share of the value of US generic imports is nearer 30%. So India ships a lot and earns little. A tax on volume then hurts more than the sales figure hints.
Risk also differs by firm. In FY26, the US made up roughly 30% of Sun Pharma's revenue, about 44% of Zydus Lifesciences' and about 46% of Aurobindo Pharma's. That spread matters when the tax lands. Worth a check before treating pharma stocks as one basket.
The Tariff Clock: 0%, Then 100%, Then 200%
On 22 July 2026, US President Donald Trump set out a phased plan for imported generics.
- Duty-free through July 2028, a two-year transition running from 1 August 2026.
- A 100% tariff from August 2028.
- 200% from 2029.
The stated aim is to move plants into the US. Markets did not wait for 2028. The Nifty Pharma index fell close to 2% intraday on the news, then won back part of the drop.
One legal detail matters. These duties would likely ride on Section 232 of the US Trade Expansion Act, which covers national security. That is firmer ground than the trade taxes struck down earlier in 2026. So the threat is not idle. SAHI tracked the first market reaction when the plan broke.
Under the July 2026 US plan, when does the 100% tariff on imported generic medicines begin?
Why Shifting Plants to America Is Not the Fix
Building in the US looks like the easy answer. The maths says no.
Land, labour, power and rules all cost more there. Generic margins are thin to start with. A plant also takes years. Firms need land, then a build, then testing, then sign-off from the FDA.
Pharmexcil puts it at five years or more to rebuild a full pharma supply chain inside the US. The taxes begin in 2028. Those dates do not line up.
The API Gap Nobody Is Pricing In
The plan covers finished generics. It says little about Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients, or APIs. These are the raw chemicals that go into a pill.
That silence is the biggest hole in the plan. About 80% of the APIs used by India's drug firms come from China. And for 83 of the top 100 generic drugs sold in the US, there is no US source of the API at all.
So a new US plant would still buy its raw inputs, most likely from China. Whether APIs get taxed later will decide how much really shifts.
Roughly what share of the Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients used by Indian drugmakers comes from China?
Three Things Investors Get Wrong Here
- Treating 2028 as far away. Supply deals with US buyers are signed years ahead. Price talks for the tax years start well before the tax does.
- Reading the US fall as lost demand. Pharmexcil blames the FY26 dip on a high base, price cuts in generics and buyers running down stock. Those things pass.
- Treating pharma as one trade. A firm earning 46% of sales from the US is not the same bet as one earning 30%. The wider India-US trade picture cuts each name a bit differently.
What to Watch Next
Pharmexcil expects 6-10% annual growth over the next three years. Double-digit growth can follow if the high-value lines deliver.
Those lines are the real story. Biosimilars, peptides, complex generics, injectables and speciality drugs all earn better margins than plain generics. Patents in the GLP-1 class start to lapse soon, and Indian firms are already lining up for it.
The other shift is on the map. Europe, Japan, Latin America and Africa are all being pushed harder. FY26 showed that this works. But none of it is quick. That is exactly why the 2030 number moved.
Sources: Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India (Pharmexcil) FY26 export data and chairman's statements; NSE Nifty Pharma index data; the US announcement of 22 July 2026; company FY26 results. Figures as of August 2026.

ai-446cf03517.headline: IIT-Madras AI4Bharat, Josh Talks AI launch AI evaluation platform tailored for Indian models
ai-446cf03517.fulltext:
AI4Bharat, an initiative from IIT-Madras alongside Josh Talks AI has launched Voice of India, a multimodal AI Evaluation platform dedicated to evaluating AI systems against real-world Indian conditions.
The platform will enable governments, enterprises, researchers and AI developers to independently assess how AI systems perform across Indian languages, accents, dialects and deployment environments.
It was launched at an event in New Delhi in the presence of S. Krishnan, Secretary, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
Rather than relying solely on performance metrics or benchmarks developed for Western contexts, the platform provides scientifically rigorous, India-specific evaluations that reflect how AI is actually used across the country, a statement from the parties, said.
According to the joint statement, the Voice of India AI Evaluation Platform will be a new layer in India’s AI ecosystem building on top of AI models, compute infrastructure and language technologies. It will evaluate models across voice, speech translation, long-document processing, including accuracy, cultural appropriateness across Indian languages and legal reasoning.
Robust evaluation
“With AI systems becoming more deeply integrated into society, rigorous evaluation becomes as important as model development itself. Through Voice of India, we hope to provide the research community, industry and policymakers with scientifically robust evaluation frameworks that reflect India’s linguistic diversity. India has a unique opportunity not only to build AI for the world, but also to help define how the world measures it,” said Mitesh Khapra, AI4Bharat, IIT Madras.
“The next frontier in AI isn’t building larger models. It’s building better ways to measure whether they actually work. The Voice of India AI Evaluation Platform aims to create independent, transparent evaluation infrastructure that helps AI builders understand where models succeed, where they fail and why,” Shobhit Banga, Co-Founder, Josh Talks AI.

ai-bd57923970.headline: Why India Needs Strategic Autonomy In AI Ecosystem
ai-bd57923970.fulltext:
August 04, 2026 19:29 IST
	
	
4 Minutes Read
IT Secretary S Krishnan outlines India's strategic vision for artificial intelligence, emphasizing the critical need for domestic capability, diversified global supply chains, and a robust regulatory framework to achieve AI autonomy and global leadership.
- India must achieve "strategic autonomy" in AI by developing strong domestic capabilities.
- Avoiding overdependence on any single technology source or location is crucial for India's AI growth.
- India aims to become a global leader in building AI-powered applications and solutions.
- The government is actively considering an artificial intelligence law and a broader regulatory framework for AI.
- Resilient and diversified AI supply chains are essential for India's integration into the global AI value chain.
India should pursue "strategic autonomy" by building enough domestic capability in key parts of the AI ecosystem and avoid overdependence on any single technology source or location, while remaining firmly integrated into trusted and verified global supply chains, IT Secretary S Krishnan said on Tuesday.
Krishnan said India has an opportunity to emerge as a global leader in building AI-powered applications and solutions for the world. He said India should leverage inputs from multiple sources while avoiding overdependence on any single country or source, and build sufficient capabilities to become an indispensable part of the global AI value chain.
"Sovereign has a particular context. I think in the Indian context, even in a global context today, the appropriate term would be strategic autonomy. So, we need to have autonomy in the way in which we build these structures," Krishnan said. He was speaking at the launch of an independent multimodal AI evaluation platform by AI4Bharat (research initiative at IIT Madras) and Josh Talks AI.
Krishnan further cautioned against overdependence on one source, or any one particular location. "And equally, we need to have some capacity domestically in order to make sure, especially in a country the size of India...in some part of this value chain, you need to have a significant presence so that you can't be taken for granted, or people can't say we are going to bypass you completely," Krishnan said.
The IT secretary spoke in favour of resilient and diversified AI supply chains, acknowledging global interdependence, while avoiding excessive reliance on any single source or place. "That is how you build interdependence and a structure where you can rely on trusted and verified sources for certain kinds of things, and you are also part of that trusted and verified supply chain with enough diversification, enough resilience so you can go through a number of situations," Krishnan said.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines, Krishnan said the time has come to start thinking about an artificial intelligence law and the broader regulatory framework that should govern the technology, and added that the government is currently in the process of gathering feedback. "I think AI law is what we mentioned...that some form of regulation of AI will have to come in at some point, and probably the time to start thinking about it is now. So we are, at this point, primarily looking at feedback," he said. Asked about the status of draft IT rules tweaks, he said, "We'll have to see which elements we look at, in case we are looking at a new statute...then whether we should take it into an Act or whether we should do it only by rules... Those are the aspects."

ai-cfc3fc8f89.headline: Children, AI, And Online Safety: India's Next Digital Rights Challenge
ai-cfc3fc8f89.fulltext:
Somewhere in India this evening, a child too young to legally sign a contract is confiding in a chatbot. Not asking it homework questions, but talking to it about loneliness, about a fight at school, about feelings an eleven-year-old rarely voices to an adult. The chatbot listens patiently, responds warmly, and remembers nothing of the legal architecture built to protect that child, because that architecture was not designed with this relationship in mind. This is the quiet frontier of India's next digital rights debate, and it is arriving faster than our institutions are prepared to answer it.
For a decade, India's child-safety conversation online was framed almost entirely around content: pornography, cyberbullying, predatory contact, data harvesting for targeted advertisement. These remain real and serious harms, and the legal system has built, however imperfectly, a response to them the POCSO Act's provisions on child sexual abuse material, the IT Act's takedown obligations, and now the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which requires verifiable parental consent before processing a child's personal data and bars behavioural tracking and targeted advertising directed at minors. But generative AI has introduced a category of harm that content-based regulation was never built to catch: relationship-based harm, where the risk lies not in what a child is shown, but in what a system persuades a child to believe, feel, or depend upon.
Companion chatbots designed for engagement, not welfare, can cultivate emotional attachment in exactly the demographic least equipped to recognise it as engineered. UNICEF's own guidance on AI and children has flagged emotional dependency on companion chatbots and AI-generated disinformation as genuinely novel risks distinct from, and in some ways harder to regulate than, the older harms of explicit content or online predators, because there is no obscene image to take down and no predator to name. The harm is diffuse, cumulative, and built into the product's design incentives.
The regulatory scaffolding exists but wasn't built for this
To be fair to policymakers, India is not starting from zero. The DPDPA's parental-consent and no-targeted-advertising provisions for children are among the more protective in comparative data law. The IT Rules amendments moving through 2026 add labelling requirements for AI-generated content and faster takedown timelines. States have begun legislating too Karnataka's draft Responsible social media and Digital Safety Bill, currently before the legislature's law department, proposes mandatory labelling of AI-generated content and platform action within 24-48 hours on harmful material. At the Centre, India's AI Governance Guidelines articulate child welfare as a design principle, and a private member's Bill in the Lok Sabha has floated mandatory ethical review for high-risk AI systems.
The trouble is that nearly all of this scaffolding is content-and-consent architecture, adapted from an internet-safety paradigm built for static websites and social media feeds. Verifiable parental consent assumes a threshold moment sign-up after which the relationship is presumed safe unless specific harmful content appears. But a companion AI's risk profile does not announce itself at sign-up. It accumulates over months of conversation, through a system optimised to maximise engagement by mirroring the child's emotional needs back at them. No consent form, however well-drafted, anticipates that.
What other jurisdictions are attempting, and why India cannot simply import them
France's approach debated recently at a New Delhi forum bringing together Indian and French policymakers has leaned toward hard age gates: barring under-15s from social platforms outright and redesigning algorithmic defaults around parental consent rather than a one-time click-through. It is a blunt instrument, and one India's own digital-inclusion realities complicate considerably. A hard age-verification regime assumes reliable identity infrastructure reaching every child uniformly, when in fact large sections of India's young population access AI-enabled devices through shared family phones, cybercafes, or school-provided tablets, where the very idea of a single verifiable “user” breaks down. Any Indian regulatory response modelled uncritically on European age-gating risks either being unenforceable at scale or, worse, becoming another documentation burden that formal, urban, digitally fluent families can navigate while rural and lower-income children are pushed toward unregulated, unlabelled alternatives precisely the exclusionary pattern India's digital governance has struggled with before.
Three things India's legal response actually needs
First, the DPDPA's child-consent framework needs an explicit AI-interaction layer, distinguishing static data collection from ongoing, adaptive, relationship-simulating systems, and imposing design obligations not just consent obligations on products marketed to or predictably used by minors. A consent checkbox cannot substitute for a duty to design conversational AI that recognises signs of distress and routes a child toward a human, rather than deeper into the product.
Second, the accountability gap between platform and model developer needs closing. Current intermediary-liability thinking, inherited from the social-media era, assigns responsibility to the platform hosting content. But a companion chatbot's harmful output is generated, not hosted the developer of the underlying model bears a design responsibility that existing IT Rules categories do not clearly capture, and India's evolving AI governance framework should say so explicitly rather than leaving it to be litigated after harm occurs.
Third, and most urgently, this cannot remain a Centre-versus-States patchwork. Karnataka's Bill and the Centre's guidelines are moving on separate tracks, with no guarantee of interoperable definitions of “AI-generated content” or “child user.” A child's protection should not depend on which State's server logs the interaction.
A narrow window
India has an unusual advantage here: it is legislating on children and AI before, not after, a defining scandal forces its hand, as social media regulation so often was. That window will not stay open. The DPDPA's child provisions, the IT Rules amendments, and the AI Governance Guidelines were each meaningful steps when drafted but each was substantially settled before companion AI became a mainstream part of a child's daily emotional life. Closing the gap between what these frameworks assume about a “child user” and what a child actually now does with AI is not a technical footnote. It is the next real test of whether India's digital rights architecture protects the people least able to protect themselves within it.
Author is an Assistant Professor at School of Law CHRIST (Deemed to be University), Delhi NCR Campus. Views are personal.

ai-cd282c0e88.headline: India, Artificial Intelligence and the New Geopolitics of Power
ai-cd282c0e88.fulltext:
Is Artificial intelligence a technological revolution, an economic opportunity or a threat to employment? It is all these things. However, for India, its deepest significance rests in that AI is becoming an organising principle of international power.
Artificial intelligence is therefore the ground zero on which the future distribution of global power may be decided. The countries that dominate advanced computing, semiconductor design, data infrastructure, frontier models and the scientific talent behind them will possess advantages extending far beyond the technology sector. They will influence military capability, industrial competitiveness, intelligence, finance, diplomacy and the rules under which the rest of the world accesses knowledge.
We are aware that previous technological transformations saw seismic change through machinery, weapons and industrial production. AI operates differently. It is a general-purpose capability embedded across economic and strategic life. Its hydra-headed qualities can accelerate scientific discovery, improve manufacturing, reshape education, strengthen surveillance, generate propaganda, identify military targets and compress the time available for decisions in a crisis. The same underlying technology can serve both civilian development and warfare.
This makes AI a complicated issue to govern. Nuclear facilities, missile deployments and conventional weapons leave identifiable physical signatures. Advanced algorithms and model weights can be copied, modified and transferred with relative ease. Civilian and military uses cannot always be separated. Traditional approaches to arms control and technology regulation may consequently prove inadequate.
The geopolitical question of who invents the most capable system is not the sole issue here. It is who commands the infrastructure beneath it.
The anatomy of AI power
Sometimes, artificial intelligence is imagined as software floating freely in the digital world. It rests upon a highly concentrated physical architecture: advanced semiconductors, manufacturing equipment, cloud platforms, data centres, electricity grids, cooling systems, undersea cables, critical minerals and specialised human talent.
Several strategic chokepoints are thus created by this architecture. The United States remains pre-eminent in frontier-model development, advanced chip design, cloud infrastructure, research universities and venture finance. Taiwan is indispensable to the manufacture of leading-edge semiconductors. The Netherlands and Japan occupy critical positions in semiconductor equipment. China combines industrial scale, state-directed investment, a large research ecosystem and growing capabilities across chips, models and applications.
A key determinant of technological power today is energy. The International Energy Agency observes that there is “no AI without energy”: Data centres that are AI-focused consume very large quantities of electricity, while the largest facilities under construction may use many times the power of a typical one. Countries able to supply reliable electricity quickly and at scale will possess a significant advantage.
The dependencies thus created turn AI supply chains into instruments of statecraft. Semiconductor export controls, restrictions on manufacturing equipment and rules governing access to advanced computing are now components of geopolitical competition. The United States has explicitly used export controls to regulate the international diffusion of advanced chips and certain powerful closed-model capabilities on national-security grounds.
For India, the first strategic reality of the AI age is this: technological interdependence is unavoidable, but excessive dependence can become a political vulnerability.
The danger of a new technological hierarchy
Will AI produce an international hierarchy resembling the discriminatory structure of the nuclear order? A small number of technological powers might preserve their lead through control over computing infrastructure and access to frontier capabilities, leaving developing countries dependent on systems whose terms they do not determine. But the analogy is not exact. AI is more commercially diffuse than nuclear technology, and open-source models make technological containment difficult. But the political danger cannot be taken lightly.
An AI order dominated by two centres of power would offer the rest of the world a very restrictive and confining choice. Countries might be asked to adopt an American or Chinese technological ecosystem, with each carrying its own hardware, cloud infrastructure, standards, cybersecurity arrangements and political assumptions. Technological choice could increasingly resemble strategic alignment.
The American system is driven principally by private corporations, frontier research and proprietary platforms, though the state exercises growing influence through defence procurement, investment rules and export controls. China’s approach combines state direction with industrial deployment, extensive public infrastructure and a strong commitment to open-source models as instruments of rapid adoption and international reach.
By no means is either model politically neutral. Technology is weighted by the assumptions of the institutions that build and govern it. Dependence on a foreign AI ecosystem can influence where data are stored, whose security standards apply, what forms of surveillance are possible and whether access can be restricted during a diplomatic dispute.
India should therefore resist the idea that the AI world can be carved neatly into American and Chinese spheres. But resistance cannot consist merely of invoking strategic autonomy. India needs sufficient capability and international leverage to keep meaningful choices open that contribute to both national security and national development.
India’s emerging position
India possesses important advantages. It has scale, a large technology workforce, a strong entrepreneurial sector, extensive digital public infrastructure and an international position that enables cooperation with both advanced and developing economies.
The India AI Mission represents an attempt to convert some of these assets into national capability. Its seven pillars include shared computing access, datasets, indigenous models, socially useful applications, skills, start-up financing and safe and trusted AI. The mission has a budgetary outlay of ₹10,372 crore, and its compute programme offers eligible users subsidised access to a diversified pool of advanced processors.
At the 2026 India AI Impact Summit, the government said that more than 38,000 GPUs had already been provisioned under the mission, with plans to add another 20,000. The summit’s declaration, endorsed by 92 countries and international organisations, placed particular emphasis on democratising AI resources, human-capital development, trustworthy systems and access for social empowerment.
These are significant measures. Yet compute rented through public-private partnerships does not by itself constitute technological sovereignty. Much of India’s advanced computing still depends on foreign-designed chips, foreign cloud infrastructure and globally concentrated supply chains. India is building semiconductor capacity, but achieving leadership at the most advanced nodes will require sustained investment, manufacturing experience, research depth and reliable access to specialised equipment.
India should avoid two illusions. One is that self-reliance requires complete technological autarky. That is impossible in an industry whose supply chains cross several continents. The other is that access to global markets makes domestic capability unnecessary. That is a strategic labyrinth that would invite grave complications.
The more realistic objective is managed interdependence: strong indigenous competence in critical areas, diversified supply chains, trusted international partnerships and enough domestic knowledge to evaluate, adapt and, when necessary, replace imported systems.
The India-US relationship
The United States will remain central to India’s AI strategy. Its corporations dominate many layers of the global technology stack, and its universities and research institutions remain vital sources of innovation and talent.
The India-US AI Opportunity Partnership announced in February 2026 explicitly identifies critical minerals, energy, computing and semiconductor manufacturing as the physical foundations of AI. It envisages cooperation in processor access, data centres, research and development, investment and trusted semiconductor ecosystems.
This partnership offers India significant advantages. It can widen access to capital, advanced chips, research networks and frontier technologies. It also fits the larger strategic convergence between India and the United States in response to China’s rise.
But the relationship will involve asymmetry. Washington’s export-control system distinguishes among partners according to security assessments and political trust. Access to advanced technology may remain conditional, revisable and vulnerable to changes in American domestic politics. US companies may invest in Indian capacity while retaining control over the most valuable intellectual property, cloud architecture and model development.
India should deepen the partnership without mistaking strategic convergence for guarantees of technological assurance. Trust is valuable, but capability remains the more durable foundation of ever-resilient autonomy.
China: competitor, neighbour and unavoidable interlocutor
China presents India with a more complicated challenge.
It is a strategic competitor and a military adversary along an unsettled border. At the same time, it is a major economic power, a dominant manufacturing centre and an increasingly capable AI nation. Its advances in affordable and open-source models may prove especially attractive to developing countries that cannot afford proprietary Western systems.
China’s strategy is not simply to produce the world’s most advanced model. It seeks to embed AI across manufacturing, logistics, robotics, surveillance, scientific research and state administration. This integration between digital intelligence and industrial capacity may become a more important benchmark of national power than spectacular performance in isolated frontier areas.
India must study this model without imitating its political features. The lesson is not that India should adopt China’s system of state control. It is that AI policy cannot be separated from industrial policy, education, energy, manufacturing and research.
A country that develops software but imports the hardware, machines, sensors and industrial systems through which AI reaches the physical economy cannot be master of what it surveys.
India should compete with China where necessary and reduce strategic dependence in sensitive sectors. Yet complete technological disengagement would be neither feasible nor wise. India and China will need channels of discussion on AI safety, military applications, cyber instability and international standards. Rival powers have often needed rules precisely because they were rivals.
Beyond the binary
India’s most promising strategy lies in a wider network of technological partnerships.
Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are critical to semiconductor and electronics supply chains. Europe offers scientific capability and a regulatory philosophy centred on risk, accountability and fundamental rights. The European Union’s AI Act uses a graduated, risk-based framework, imposing stronger obligations on high-risk systems and powerful general-purpose models.
France, Germany, the Netherlands and the Nordic countries can be valuable partners in research, manufacturing, energy-efficient computing and governance. Singapore offers regulatory and technological sophistication. The Gulf states bring capital, energy and ambitions to become major

ISRO Robotics Challenge Drives Students Towards Future Space Missions
He encouraged students to become creators of technology, rather than merely its users, and to pursue ambitious engineering challenges without fear of failure: Reports
NELLORE: Months of experimentation, repeated redesigns, and extensive field testing culminated in the third edition of the Isro Robotics Challenge–URSC (IRoC-U) 2026, where teams of students showcased autonomous systems designed to simulate future planetary explorations.
Organised by the UR Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), the competition attracted nearly 590 teams from across the country, 20 of them qualifying for the final field round held in Bengaluru from July 21 to July 23. The 2026 edition, themed — Towards Swarm Expedition: Autonomous Surveyor Challenge for Exploration, Navigation and Dynamics (ASCEND) —required participants to develop a fully autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and base station capable of surveying terrain, navigating, detecting features, landing autonomously, transferring data, and recharging in a GPS-denied environment, similar to conditions expected during planetary missions.
The finalists demonstrated solutions integrating artificial intelligence, robotics, computer vision, autonomous navigation, and embedded systems before Isro scientists and experts. Addressing the valedictory ceremony, Isro chairman and Space department secretary V. Narayanan said the participants represent the future of India's space programme.
Recalling India’s journey from transporting rocket components on bicycles and bullock carts to achieving missions, such as the Mars Orbiter Mission, Chandrayaan-3, SpaDeX and NISAR, he said perseverance, teamwork, and confidence in indigenous capabilities have driven the country's space achievements.
He encouraged students to become creators of technology, rather than merely its users, and to pursue ambitious engineering challenges without fear of failure. URSC director M. Sankaran said the competition intended not only to identify winners but also build technical competence, creativity, teamwork, and confidence among young engineers by exposing them to real-world engineering challenges. Chief evaluator V. Koteswara Rao described the event as a "festival of innovation.”
He commended the quality of autonomous systems developed by the participants. Launched in 2024 to commemorate the successful soft landing of Chandrayaan-3 near the Moon's South Pole, IRoC-U has evolved into a national platform connecting students with innovation and technologies relevant to India's future space exploration programmes.
The winners of IRoC-U 2026 will be announced on National Space Day on August 23.

india-deep-tech-ee166fcd93.headline: Mitsubishi Electric Backs Quantum Optimization Startup JIJ via ¥5B CVC Fund
india-deep-tech-ee166fcd93.fulltext:
Mitsubishi Electric Backs Quantum Optimization Startup JIJ via ¥5B CVC Fund
KEY POINTS
- Mitsubishi Electric invests in quantum optimization startup JIJ through the ME Innovation Fund
- Tie-up combines JIJ's JijZept middleware platform with Mitsubishi Electric's quantum and software development strengths
- Investment becomes the 15th deal for the 5 billion yen fund run with Global Brain
Mitsubishi Electric has invested in JIJ, a Japanese startup that develops and provides middleware for mathematical optimization using quantum computers and other technologies, as the 15th investment from its corporate venture capital fund jointly operated with Global Brain, the company said on Aug. 4.
The Japanese industrial group aims to accelerate research and development toward early social implementation of quantum technologies by combining JIJ's middleware and development environment with Mitsubishi Electric's application development, software implementation and quantum technologies, including work on interconnection technology between quantum computers.
JIJ develops and provides JijZept, a platform designed to let users address a range of business issues through mathematical optimization without requiring specialist expertise. Mathematical optimization refers to the use of mathematical methods and algorithms to determine minimum or maximum values under given constraints, while middleware is software that sits between an operating system and applications and provides common functions such as communications processing, database connectivity and data conversion.
JIJ was founded in 2018 and is based in Tokyo's Minato Ward. In addition to JijZept, the company supports the launch, planning and execution of mathematical optimization projects and develops software and middleware for the use of quantum computing.
Mitsubishi Electric said quantum computing is moving from the research stage toward practical use, with technology development for industrial applications accelerating. The company has positioned quantum computing as a priority area in its research and development strategy and has been advancing work on the social implementation of quantum technologies.
JIJ Chief Executive Yu Yamashiro said in the statement that the company had worked to make complex industrial issues computationally tractable using mathematical optimization and quantum computing technologies, and would seek to further industrial applications by combining its strengths with Mitsubishi Electric's expertise in quantum-related technologies.
The investment was made through the ME Innovation Fund, formally registered as ME Innovation Investment Limited Partnership. The fund was established by Mitsubishi Electric and Global Brain with total capital of 5 billion yen and a 10-year duration. Global Brain is the fund's general partner, while Mitsubishi Electric is its limited partner. It invests in domestic and overseas startups with potential for collaboration with Mitsubishi Electric, mainly in digital and green innovation fields.
Mitsubishi Electric has been stepping up corporate venturing activity, with sequential investments totaling 10 billion yen since fiscal 2020. The group posted consolidated revenue of 5.8947 trillion yen for fiscal 2025 and has more than 200 group companies and about 150,000 employees worldwide.

As US and China compete over AI, middle powers can craft a third path
Between American-secured diffusion and Chinese developmental multilateralism, middle powers have space to make their presence felt
The global AI race is becoming a contest over the international order. In June, the US convened the second summit under the 24-economy Pax Silica around secure supply chains, AI infrastructure and trusted technology partnerships. In July, all 193 UN member states met in Geneva for the inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
The American pathway is built around control of the technological frontier. US companies dominate advanced chip design, cloud platforms, proprietary models and much of the software used to train and deploy AI. Washington is organising these assets through Pax Silica, full-stack export packages, public finance, semiconductor partnerships and cybersecurity networks. Access is widened among trusted partners while the most consequential capabilities remain subject to restrictions.
This system offers partners high-performance technology, mature firms and deep capital markets. It also creates dependence on American licences, cloud services, model updates and policy continuity. American influence therefore rests as much on the conditions of access as on the technologies themselves.
China’s offer appeals to governments seeking affordable models, local deployment and fewer alliance-based entry conditions. Yet maintenance, equipment compatibility, data practices, technical standards and supplier relationships may leave partner states dependent on Chinese systems even when models are locally operated. WAICO’s influence will depend on whether it develops a stable budget, functioning secretariat and credible projects beyond diplomatic declarations.

When Liao Heng joined Huawei Technologies’ chip-design unit in 2016, he was sceptical about whether China could ever build world-class semiconductors.
A former child prodigy who entered Beijing’s prestigious Tsinghua University in 1987 at age 14 before moving to Princeton University for postdoctoral research, Liao had spent over a decade in the United States watching what he described as a “long sunset” for American chip start-ups.
Working abroad, he noted, often bred a “blind arrogance” that only Western firms were capable of true innovation. His perception changed rapidly once he witnessed Huawei’s execution first hand.
“Reality taught me a quick lesson,” Liao said on a business podcast that has recently gone viral. He noted that the chip unit, HiSilicon, finalised designs for – or “taped out” – dozens of new chips annually without a single failure to reach mass production.
“Such a high hit rate shows that every team [at the company] is highly qualified.”
Today, as chief scientist of Huawei’s semiconductor business and the chief architect behind its Ascend artificial intelligence (AI) processors, Liao stands at the centre of China’s drive for technological self-reliance.

indian-startups-42b14e4790.headline: Agentic AI Startup Kily Raises ₹30 Cr To Accelerate Platform Deployment
indian-startups-42b14e4790.fulltext: AI startup Kily has raised a ₹30 Cr ($3.2 Mn) in a funding round led by early stage VC firm Sorin Investments. Other investors that partook in the round included IPO-bound fintech major Razorpay and VC firm Wyser Capital. Kily will use the fresh capital to strengthen its product capabilities and go-to-market initiatives, as well as accelerate platform adoption for major Indian consumer brands. Founded in 2025 by ex-Flipkart and Affle executives Sankalp Mehrotra, Anurag Singh, and Sharad Chitlangia, Kily develops autonomous AI agents to help consumer brands drive growth on ecommerce and quick commerce startups. The startup claims it has already partnered with leading brands including FMCG major ITC. Its agents integrate real-time signals from marketplaces with the client brand’s objectives, operating constraints, and context to automate workflows and decide. It can help brands optimise variables like product visibility, advertising efficiency, pricing and inventory availability. “Brands and online sellers today operate in an increasingly fragmented ecosystem, where growth and profitability depend on making thousands of decisions across marketplaces every day. Kily is built to bring autonomy to commerce management, enabling brands and their partners to execute faster, make better decisions and scale profitably,” cofounder and CEO Mehrotra said. The investment comes at a time when businesses across industries are aggressively turning towards AI to streamline operations and manual workflows. And investors are increasingly taking note of platforms providing such solutions. In the Indian context, there’s no better example than that of Emergent, whose AI agents allow entrepreneurs and small businesses to build software and websites without deep technical knowledge or experience. The startup became India’s third homegrown AI unicorn and sixth unicorn of 2026 when it raised $130 Mn in a Series C funding round earlier this year. Another prominent name in the emerging Indian AI space is Sarvam, which also joined the unicorn club this year after raising $234 Mn as part of its $300 Mn Series B funding round. Additionally, the startup hosted the first edition of its developer conference, Sarvam Epoch, this week, where it unveiled its ambitions of building an end-to-end AI stack. Freehand, a startup focusing on agentic AI for enterprise supply chain operations, raised $75 Mn just last week as well. Zooming out, Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in the first half of 2026, per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report’. This capital inflow amounted to a 4X jump compared to the same period last year.

indian-startups-c805821d4e.headline: AI-Native CRM Startup Superleap Bags ₹36 Cr Led By Peak XV’s Surge
indian-startups-c805821d4e.fulltext: Enterprise tech startup Superleap has raised ₹36 Cr (around $4.2 Mn) in its pre-Series A funding round led by Peak XV Partners’ Surge. The Bengaluru-based startup said it will use the fresh capital to expand its enterprise go-to-market efforts, accelerate adoption of AI-native customer relationship management (CRM) platforms in India, and strengthen its product and platform capabilities. Founded in 2024 by former Unacademy executives Subham Kumar Boundia, Alok Maurya, and Saurabh Maheshwari, Superleap is building an AI-native CRM platform for enterprise revenue teams. Positioning itself as an alternative to legacy CRM platforms, the startup claims it can reduce deployment timelines from months to weeks while enabling enterprises to migrate without disrupting business operations. Its platform comprises SuperOS, a unified data layer powering enterprise intelligence, and SuperAgents, an agentic layer that automates tasks across the revenue cycle. The platform also includes AI voice bots, conversational intelligence, Superleap AI, and MCP integrations with tools such as WhatsApp, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Claude, and ChatGPT. Its Superleap Deploy is designed to help enterprises migrate from legacy CRM systems through its forward-deployed engineering model. The startup claims to have grown 10X over the past year and built a customer base spanning BFSI, SaaS, education, healthcare, travel and hospitality, and media. Its customers include Razorpay, Aakash Education, MediBuddy, HCL GUVI, Cars24, PagarBook, Plum, Qube Cinema, and Superhealth. Highlighting customer deployments, Superleap said Razorpay migrated more than 10 Mn records to its platform within 45 days without business disruption. It added that Aakash Education transitioned nearly 5,000 counsellors across 400 locations in under 60 days. The funding comes amid growing enterprise demand for AI-native software that goes beyond traditional record-keeping to automate workflows and improve revenue generation. SaaS startups across CRM, sales automation, ERP, billing, and human resource management are increasingly pitching AI-first alternatives to legacy enterprise software. For instance, AI-powered SaaS startup Kris@Work raised $3 Mn in its seed round earlier this yea to offer an agentic AI-based, end-to-end platform for go-to-market (GTM) teams, including sales, marketing, revenue, and growth, to eliminate the need for multiple SaaS tools. indian-startups-e22525beca.headline: GetVantage Raises ₹63 Cr To Expand Its B2B Revenue Based Financing Platform
indian-startups-e22525beca.fulltext: B2B fintech startup GetVantage has raised ₹63 Cr (about $6.6 Mn) in a Series A1 funding round to expand its finance platform and increase its committed financing capacity. The round, which constituted both equity and debt, was led by ex-RBL Bank MD Rajeev Ahuja and investment firm SanRaj Group. Existing investors including Chiratae Ventures, Varanium Fintech Fund, and VCMint also participated in the round. With the latest round, the startup has raised over $47 Mn in funding till date from investors like Varanium Capital Advisors, InCred Capital, Sony Innovation Fund, among others. The Mumbai-based startup said the fresh capital will be used to scale its capital gateway platform, an API-led infrastructure that enables marketplaces and logistics companies to embed financing solutions for their merchant networks. Founded in 2019 by Amit Srivastava and Bhavik Vasa, GetVantage initially focused on revenue-based financing and has since expanded into cash-flow-based lending solutions for MSMEs. GetVantage offers data-driven growth capital and embedded finance solutions ranging from ₹2 Lakh up to ₹20 Cr for startups, MSMEs, and ecommerce players. It provides equity-free funding through revenue-sharing agreements where repayments scale with monthly sales. The platform uses alternative data and analytics to evaluate businesses based on their cash flows rather than relying only on collateral or traditional lending criteria. Its financing products include term loans, business loans, and cash advances tailored to the operating cycles of small businesses. The startup claims that its capital gateway platform helps connect institutional capital with underserved MSMEs by enabling customised credit solutions through cash-flow-based underwriting and digital lending. For context, a capital gateway is a B2B fintech infrastructure layer that connects businesses to instant working capital. The platform claims to have aided over 2,000 businesses including Arata, Rage Coffee, The Healthy Company, and Elevar. The investment comes at a time when the Indian MSME sector faces a credit gap of around ₹30 Lakh Cr, as small businesses struggle to access formal financing due to challenges such as collateral requirements, limited credit history, and documentation hurdles. This gap has created opportunities for fintech startups to build digital lending platforms using alternative data, cash-flow-based underwriting, and embedded finance models to enable faster access to working capital for MSMEs. In this ecosystem, GetVantage competes with other revenue-based financing and alternative lending platforms including Velocity, Klub, Efficient Capital Labs, among others.

Founded in 2025 by Chinmay Bhosale and Vikrant Labde, the startup develops AI infrastructure for legal and compliance work. Its platform includes tools for legal research, document drafting and summarisation, contract review and regulatory compliance.
NYAI said its technology can be integrated with an organisation’s existing large language models while allowing sensitive legal information to remain within the organisation’s own infrastructure. The startup claimed that its system provides citation-backed results and is designed to prioritise legal accuracy, traceability and accountability.
“In a jurisdiction as layered as ours, a tool is not an answer,” Bhosale said.
He added that law firms and in-house legal teams needed infrastructure they could control, with workflows tailored to their own legal practices rather than a technology provider’s standard system.

By Canary Media
                            Valar, which has been called “the Trump administration’s favorite nuclear startup,” faces a steep path to realizing its vision — even with a giant funding round.
                        
                    
                    Valar Atomics, the three-year-old microreactor developer that has a forged a close relationship with the Trump administration, has raised $1 billion in its Series B funding round as investors increasingly bet that the White House’s overhaul of nuclear regulations will clear the way for the country’s first big atomic buildout in more than half a century.
On Monday, the Torrance, California–based startup announced its latest funding round, led by venture capital giant Sequoia, will be used to lay the groundwork for commercialization of Valar’s 5-megawatt Ward 250 reactor, which uses helium as a coolant instead of water. The reactor design has yet to receive approval from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
“So, what does the new Series B financing mean for Valar? It allows us to make the next mission critical evolution: Valar will transition from demonstrating the operability of an integrated reactor system to producing fleets of them en masse,” Valar founder and CEO Isaiah Taylor said in a post on the company website. “This has been Valar’s mission since its inception.”
It’s a milestone for a company that once drew derision within the nuclear industry over audacious claims its 27-year-old founder made on social media to back up a lawsuit against the NRC. The young executive’s showmanship, shrouded in patriotic language, attracted attention from Republican officials. Before long, Valar had emerged as what Mother Jones called “the Trump administration’s favorite nuclear startup.”
Last August, the Department of Energy selected Valar as one of 10 companies to take part in a new pilot program that aimed to help next-generation reactor startups split atoms for the first time. A month later, the agency named the company as one of four to take part in a separate pilot program to develop new supply chains for nuclear fuel. Two months after that, Valar became the first venture-backed startup to split atoms using an experimental core at Los Alamos National Laboratory.
In February, Valar made history by loading the parts for its Ward 250 onto a C-17 Globemaster III aircraft at the March Air Reserve Base in California and flying them to Utah’s Hill Air Force Base. The airlift, touted by the Trump administration as “groundbreaking,” was the first demonstration that a microreactor could be wholly transported by plane. In June, Valar split atoms with its prototype Ward 250, becoming the second company in the pilot program to do so.
The new funding, the company said Monday, will allow it “to fully execute a vertically integrated, hardware first approach; one that encompasses everything from reactor deployment and long-term operations to fuel production.”
The company faces significant hurdles to realize that vision. The U.S. operated what’s known as a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor back in the 1970s. The Fort St. Vrain nuclear station, Colorado’s only such facility, shut down after a decade of costly maintenance issues and outages. It was replaced with a natural gas–fired plant. A handful of similar reactors have been built around the world, but primarily operated as experimental units.
China started construction on its first major high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in 2012, and split atoms for the first time in 2021. But Beijing really reignited the race to commercialize the technology, which could help avoid tricky questions around using water for cooling, in December 2023. That’s when China’s first 150-megawatt, helium-cooled reactor began selling electricity to the grid. Two years later, China launched a new industrial alliance to hasten the development of high-temperature gas-cooled reactors. In January, Beijing kicked off construction on its second such reactor, which will have four times the capacity of the first one.
At a moment when Europe’s heat wave is forcing inland nuclear stations cooled with river water to cut production, high-temperature gas-cooled reactors look particularly promising.
But developers of small modular reactors, which produce less than 300 megawatts each, and microreactors, which produce less than 20 megawatts each, still need to prove that the technology makes economic sense. Historically, reactor companies have increased profits by building larger, higher-output units — not by selling a high volume of smaller ones.
Valar also intends to manufacture its own fuel. That comes with its own steep challenges, particularly since the company is using a complex fuel form known as TRISO. Currently, only a handful of domestic suppliers are working to ramp up production.
Even if Valar can secure the fuel it needs and prove that assembly-line reproduction is good business, the company will still face competition from serious contenders with deep-pocketed backers.
Kairos Power, which broke ground on its first plant in Tennessee earlier this year, is backed by Google. X-energy, in which Amazon took an equity stake in 2024, won a key federal approval for its first project in May.
Neither of those companies is seen as having particular political leanings. But Valar’s ties to the Trump administration, a boon today, could become a liability whenever Democrats retake power.
Already, President Donald Trump’s personal ties to the nuclear industry are inviting scrutiny. Valar’s latest fundraising may only add more. The Sequoia partner who led the fundraising round is Shaun Maguire, a vocal Trump supporter who became a lightning rod last year over controversial remarks he made that were widely condemned as bigoted against Muslims. Maguire will join Valar’s board as part of the deal. 
Alexander C. Kaufman is a contributing reporter at Canary Media, and an award-winning writer who has covered energy and climate change for more than a decade.

climate-energy-da2c26b887.headline: Editorial Analysis: Transmission Bottlenecks in India’s Renewable Sector
climate-energy-da2c26b887.fulltext:
GS-3: Renewable energy
Introduction:
The Sustainable Project Developers Association (SPDA) urged the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) to provide financial relief after 8,133 GWh of solar power was curtailed during April–June 2026 due to transmission delays.
About Transmission Bottlenecks in India’s Renewable Sector:
What it is?
- Transmission bottlenecks occur when the growth rate of renewable energy (RE) capacity addition drastically outpaces the construction and commissioning of dedicated high-voltage inter-state transmission system (ISTS) lines.
- Because solar and wind projects are built within 12–18 months while transmission lines take 36–60 months, clean energy power plants are forced to operate under Temporary General Network Access (T-GNA).
- Under T-GNA, generators can inject power only when spare transmission margin exists, resulting in severe power curtailment during peak generation hours.
Key Data & Statistics:
- Massive Capacity Under Temporary Access: Approximately 21 GW (nearly 9%) of India’s installed renewable energy capacity relies on temporary grid connections (T-GNA), with 12 GW facing active evacuation limits during peak solar hours.
- High Generation Curtailment: In FY2025–26, around 6,900 GWh of clean electricity was restricted due to grid mismatches, while Q1 FY2026–27 alone saw 8,133 GWh curtailed.
- Extreme Regional Curtailments: In solar hubs like Rajasthan, RE projects experience extreme generation curtailments ranging between 70% and 95% during peak afternoon hours.
- Execution Deficit in Transmission: India met only about 80% of its annual transmission build-out targets over the past five years, with 1 in 4 major inter-state transmission schemes delayed by a year or more.
Reasons for Transmission Bottlenecks:
- Mismatched Project Timelines: Solar and wind farms can be commissioned in 12–18 months, whereas transmission lines require 36–60 months due to civil construction and equipment procurement.
Example: Solar plants in Rajasthan came online years before their dedicated ISTS pooling sub-stations were commissioned.
- Right-of-Way (RoW) and Land Disputes: Acquiring continuous corridors for high-voltage transmission lines faces intense resistance from local landowners and farmers.
Example: Line construction routinely gets halted in agricultural belts over land compensation claims.
- Forest and Environmental Clearances: Transmission corridors traversing eco-sensitive zones face prolonged regulatory hurdles.
Example: Power line construction in Rajasthan and Gujarat faced long delays to comply with Great Indian Bustard (GIB) undergrounding mandates.
- Supply Chain Shortages for HVDC Equipment: Global supply chain bottlenecks have created a shortage of critical electrical equipment.
Example: A thin global supplier base has delayed the delivery of High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) transformers and circuit breakers.
- Geographical Concentration of Generation: Renewable capacity is heavily concentrated in specific resource-rich regions rather than distributed evenly.
Example: Mass capacity additions in Rajasthan (Northern Grid) and Gujarat (Western Grid) cause severe congestion at regional grid pooling stations.
Challenges Associated with Transmission Bottlenecks:
- Imminent Financial Stress and NPA Risks: Severe curtailments reduce plant revenues to less than 5% of projections, leaving developers unable to service institutional debt.
Example: A 300 MW plant operating at 10 MW generation capacity risks turning into a Non-Performing Asset (NPA).
- Erosion of Investor Confidence & Project IRRs: Unpredictable T-GNA curtailment lowers project Internal Rates of Return (IRRs), discouraging foreign and private capital investments.
Example: Clean energy funds face lower-than-projected returns on capital deployed in Northern Grid solar parks.
- Systemic Exposure for Public Financial Institutions: Indian banks and financial institutions (such as PFC, REC, and IREDA) have deployed over ₹5.08 lakh crore in the RE sector over two financial years, creating systemic banking sector exposure.
- Wasted Clean Power & Carbon Offsets: Curtailing clean electricity forces grid operators to maintain fossil-fuel spinning reserves to meet demand.
Example: The 8,133 GWh of solar power curtailed in Q1 FY27 could have powered nearly 1.4 million homes for a year.
- Threat to National 500 GW Clean Energy Target: Persistent evacuation bottlenecks jeopardize India’s target of reaching 500 GW of non-fossil fuel power capacity by 2030.
Initiatives Taken So Far:
- Implementation of GNA Regulations: Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) rolled out the General Network Access (GNA) framework to provide firm, long-term transmission rights to ISTS-connected power plants.
- Green Energy Corridors (GEC): Implemented dedicated GEC Phase-I and Phase-II schemes to evacuate renewable power through intra-state and inter-state transmission networks.
- Scale-Up of ISTS Infrastructure Targets: Expanded future ISTS construction targets to 25,146 circuit kilometers (ckm) for FY2026–27 to clear transmission backlogs.
- Introduction of T-GNA Stopgap Arrangement: Allowed temporary grid access protocols to prevent fully constructed renewable plants from remaining completely idle while waiting for long-term transmission lines.
Way Forward:
- Co-Optimal Planning of Generation and Transmission: Shift away from generation-led planning toward synchronized, joint execution of RE plants and transmission corridors.
- Deploying Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) at Pooling Stations: Install 3–4 GW of 2-hour battery storage at congested pooling stations to absorb peak afternoon solar generation and release it during evening peak hours.
- Financial Relief and Debt Restructuring: Implement RBI-backed debt restructuring, principal repayment moratoriums, and concessional bridge financing for projects affected by transmission delays.
- Adopting Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) and Reconductoring: Utilize DLR technology and advanced conductor materials to increase the transfer capacity of existing power lines without waiting for new construction.
- Harmonizing Curtailment Compensation Frameworks: Establish standardized compensation protocols for T-GNA projects facing transmission-led backing down to protect developer revenue streams.
Conclusion:
Transmission bottlenecks pose an operational risk to India’s clean energy expansion and financial stability. Addressing this challenge requires synchronized transmission planning, rapid deployment of battery storage, and debt relief for affected developers. Aligning grid expansion with renewable generation capacity is vital to safeguard investments and achieve India’s 2030 climate goals.
